items.evidence: The overview's first section after the title is '## The bottom line', whose three paragraphs open '**1. What FRUS answers directly.**', '**2. Where FRUS points for the rest.**' and '**3. What this request cannot get from FRUS.**' in that order (lines 5, 7, 9). '**Scope.**' and '## Decisions this needs from you' follow, and '## Findings' begins only at line 22, so no finding precedes the three parts. The collection's introductionText repeats the same three parts in the same order.

Every figure carries its set and base in words: 'The argument rests on 23 printed documents, drawn from about 4,900 documents in the editors' own Cuba chapters and about 13,900 documents that mention Cuba anywhere, in the 553 volumes indexed'; 'All 553 volumes of the series as indexed, 311,429 documents once front matter, editors' notes and the duplicate second editions are set aside: 13,899 of them mention Cuba (in 481 volumes) and 4,897 sit in the editors' own Cuba chapters (62 volumes, 1900–1980)'; the vocabulary counts are ratios of 'the Cuba chapter documents' by decade ('in none of the 44 chapter documents from the 1980s', 'about one in three in the 1960s in both'); the method counts are 'about one in fifteen of the dated documents in the 1870s, one in thirteen in the 1890s, one in forty-five in the 1940s, one in nine in the 1960s' and 'About five in six of the Cuba chapter documents from 1950 on'; the zero is 'before 1940 the phrase appears in only eight such documents' out of 'every document that mentions Cuba, Cuban or Havana in all 553 volumes', and the search 'returns about 2,600 in all, almost all after 1950'. The only percentage is inside an 1886 quotation and carries its base ('buys about 95 per cent, of the sugar exported from Cuba'); the two dollar figures are the documents' own and are attributed ('the Cuban ambassador's note of 1929 claiming nearly 1,500 million dollars of American capital in Cuba ... Cuba's claim, not an American estimate'; 'American claims for expropriated property came to about two billion dollars', the Treasury Secretary's figure). Lot numbers, entry numbers, NARA identifiers and '27 linear feet' describe named archival series, not measurements of the corpus.

All 23 documents are cited to the printed series with a history.state.gov link, and none by a bare id pair or title alone. Sixteen carry series, years, title, volume and document number, e.g. '(Foreign Relations of the United States, 1961–1963, Volume XI, Cuban Missile Crisis and Aftermath, Document 21, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1961-63v11/d21)', '(Foreign Relations of the United States, 1934, The American Republics, Volume V, Document 127, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1934v05/d127)', '(Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969–1976, Volume E–10, Documents on American Republics, 1969–1972, Document 205, ...)'. Seven (1874, 1881, 1886, the 1897 Woodford despatch, the 1898 presidential message, the 1904 proclamation and the 1930 Stimson press memorandum) give series, year, volume where one exists, and the document's printed heading and date in place of a number, e.g. '(Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1874, Mr. Fish to Mr. Cushing, 6 February 1874, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1874/d552)' and '(Papers Relating to the Foreign Relations of the United States, 1930, Volume II, Memorandum of Conference by the Secretary of State with the Press, 2 October 1930, https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1930v02/d747)'; the collection's note on the first explains why ('Index number 552; the printed number is 550'), and the 1898 message is a chapter-level text with no number ('.../frus1898/ch83'). A stricter reading that demands a document number on every citation would fail those seven; none of them is a bare id pair or a title alone, which are the failures the item names.

The central zero is a described, controlled search: 'I searched every document that mentions Cuba, Cuban or Havana in all 553 volumes for the phrase, and before 1940 the phrase appears in only eight such documents, none of which uses it about Cuba's bearing on American safety (they concern wartime bond acts, disarmament talks, the Paris peace conference and a Colombian coast-guard request); the search could return hits (it returns about 2,600 in all, almost all after 1950), a search for a phrase that should be everywhere returned documents in every decade, and a search for a nonsense string returned none.' The second gap is a search with its terms and set ('I searched the Cuba documents of 1910–1935 for the words American investments and American capital; one document gives a total, and it is the Cuban ambassador's claim of 1929, not an American estimate'), the fourth a count ('the library holds two documents that mention Cuba dated 1989, both from January, and none later'), and the fifth is labelled as not measured ('I did not try to measure them'). Only the third (Cuban and Spanish views 'are not in FRUS and not in the bundled shelf lists') is an assertion, about the nature of the series rather than a count. 'How this was done' adds the general controls: 'tested the common word groups against a nonsense string and a phrase that should appear everywhere'.

No SQL, no table or column name and no file path appear anywhere in the overview. Volume/document id strings occur only inside the history.state.gov links that J3 requires (e.g. 'https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1961-63v10-12mSupp/d729'), never as a bare citation. 'file numbers beginning 837 through 1949 and 737 from 1950' are the State Department's decimal classes in Record Group 59, not paths. The method is in reader language: 'the numerical fingerprints that summarise each document's meaning', 'the index treats related word forms as the same word'. (Outside J5's scope but received by the historian: the collection's notes carry method residue such as 'a near-duplicate found by vector distance of 4 bits', 'Hamming distance 32 and 50', 'Not in the vector index, which has no row for this chapter-level text', and '106 bits from the Mallory memo, no closer than a median 25th neighbour'.)

judge:v3.rankingReason: v3 first: a 1874–1981 narrative on 23 documents quoted in-line under full printed citations with links (Fish 1874 'one great cause of perpetual solicitude', Woodford's sugar case, the Platt text, Grau's refusal of bases, Mallory's 'weaken the economic life', McNamara's 'not at all', Haig 1981), a controlled zero for 'national security' with positive and negative controls, a decade-by-decade vocabulary count against the whole series, and a collection whose 23 documents and 35 excerpts match the overview exactly; its reader-facing flaws are method residue in the collection's notes (Hamming distances, 'vector index', 'about 100,000 characters'), an excerpt that begins mid-clause ('which buys about 95 per cent,'), and a slip that calls the 1903 Treaty of Relations 'the treaty of 1904' (the note even dates it '22 May 1904'). v2 second: its random-sample-per-decade baseline is the sounder measurement and it has the 1961 task force, Cienfuegos and Mariel documents v3 lacks, but its bottom line cites by short form with no series name or link ('1902, Document 313; 1903, Document 331; 1906, Part I, Document 427'), it twice sends the historian to 'the memo' she will never open ('(see the memo)', '(thin counts; see the memo)'), it leaks tool talk ('the offline tools cannot resolve', 'the app's bundled finding aids', 'the app's document-similarity vectors'), and its sixteen documents give the 1870s only an 1870 trade report while admitting the Ten Years' War instruction 'was also not found'.

refute:v3.fabricationDetails: None. overview.md has 30 double-quoted spans; 29 are document passages (the 30th is the collection's title) and every one passes the segment-strict check (lower-case, [a-z0-9] only, split at ellipses, segments in order at increasing offsets) against header||dateline||source_note||body_text of the pair named by the URL that follows it, which is also the pair the memo's trace table (rows 29-49, M4 Q01-Q35) gives. All 35 collection excerpts pass the same check against their own volumeId/documentId (the app's checker does not test excerpts, so I ran the check myself). No overview quotation contains an ellipsis (the memo table's ellipses are width cuts; Q06 is given in full in both files). Beyond the task's list I also checked the single-quoted 'strategic concept' in Finding 4's heading against frus1952-54v04/d342 and the eight single-quoted phrases in the collection's notes and prose ('the one great cause of perpetual solicitude', 'key to the Gulf', 'for its own defense', 'constant menace', 'a strategic concept', 'not at all', 'an entirely different impact', 'The Decline and Fall of Castro'): all present in their documents.
refute:v3.miscitationDetails: None. Each overview quotation sits in the document whose URL follows it, and that URL is the memo's pair. All 23 printed citations resolve to the URL's pair: the 16 'Document N' citations match document_number exactly (127, 299, 924, 119, 878, 741, 342, 70, 112, 499, 21, 34, 729, 205, 21, 5); frus1930v02/d747 is headed 'Memorandum of Conference by the Secretary of State With the Press on October 2, 1930'; the 1874, 1881 and 1886 citations name correspondent and date and match the headers 'No. 550. Mr. Fish to Mr. Cushing.' (1874-02-06), 'No. 401. Mr. Blaine to Mr. Comly.' (1881-12-01) and 'No. 409. Mr. Curry to Mr. Bayard.' (1886-10-22) -- the printed despatch numbers (550/401/409) differ from the ids (d552/d405/d414), the overview quotes no number, and the d552 note says so; frus1898/d498 is 'Mr. Woodford to Mr. Sherman.' dated 1897-10-05; frus1898/ch83 is headed 'Message', dated 1898-04-12, and opens 'To the Congress of the United States ... the neighboring island of Cuba'; frus1904/d207 is the President's proclamation of the treaty. Manifest titles match the printed series titles. One looseness, not a mis-citation: the overview calls d207 'The treaty of 1904'; the proclamation is dated 2 July 1904 and the printed text itself says the treaty was signed at Habana 'the twenty-second day of May, one thousand nine hundred and four' (the collection note's '22 May 1904' follows the document; the treaty was historically signed in 1903).

operations: nearest neighbours of a document (vec3.py): k=15 by Hamming over the 512-bit sign block of semantic-vectors-binary.bin for six anchors
semantic join (vec3.py): each neighbour's (volume_id, document_id) joined to document_cache and document_dates for date, header, apparatus flags and 'cuba' in text
centroid similarity (vec4.py): cosine of dequantised int8 volume centroids from the corpus binary, 553 volumes, read against 2,000 random volume pairs
the map (vec4.py, vec5.py): semantic-map.bin placements and semantic-map-index.json clusters for the anchors and the Scope A cluster mix by decade, with an era-matched unclustered baseline
near-duplicates (vec6.py): Hamming of frus1881/d405 vs frus1894app2/d394 (4) and pairwise Hamming over the 22 collection documents in the index

score:v3.notes: All four files were present (memo.md, overview.md, collection.fruscollection, queries.log) along with the run's scripts and outputs. I verified the output's claims against the read-only index copy and the bundled artifacts rather than taking them from the files: the coverage figures, 311,429, 13,899|481, 2,643, the two 1989 documents, Set A (4,897 in 62 volumes; all non-apparatus, no Ed2), both archival channels (4,707; 711 citations in 501 documents from 28 volumes), every NAID and entry number in central-files-index.json, the vocabulary cells and decade rates, all 35 quotations, the 35 collection excerpts and 23 documents, the overview's 30 quoted spans and 23 URLs, and, from my own decode of the index segments, every vector figure (Hamming 4/52/32/106/61, random-pair mean 167.1 sd 14.8, neighbour medians 80 and 104, centroid cosines, 88,059 unclustered, 1,920 of 2,263). Everything reproduced. The two violations are form failures in the memo: P5 (a bare '98% in the 1970s' and a bare 'top volume share of N' column) and V6 (centroid cosines given neither through the scoreCalibration offsets nor labelled raw). Four items are obeyed with a recorded caveat an adjudicator may weigh differently: V1 (the shards manifest is not named; the session checked all 553 shard headers and .generation instead, and the manifest's digest is identical), V2 (no named row-addressable spot check; identity was confirmed on the known reprint pair at Hamming 4), S3 (splits reported as strict vs tolerant for six terms/groups but not per spelling for the Cuba forms, where habana alone is 3,079 documents), and O3 (the bottom line's part 1 defers its citations to the findings). Two quality observations outside the rubric: the overview compares 'nearly two in three' (Cuba chapters, a literal regex of communist/soviet/missile) against 'about half' of the whole series (an FTS stem group that also includes subversion), two different counting surfaces; and the bottom line says 'five distinct ways of thinking' over six numbered findings. The vector work was real (index, binary, map and all 553 shard headers opened; no Tier-2 reranking), so V1–V6 were scored, not set not_applicable.
